cards.prompt: You opened `example.com` a minute ago. Now you open it again, and your device needs its [[IP address]] once more. Where's the **fastest** place to find it?

options.text: In your own device's memory of answers it got recently
By asking the server that runs example.com's website
options.nudge: That server could be on the other side of the world. Is there somewhere closer that saw this answer a minute ago?

options.text: By searching one big list of every name on the internet
options.nudge: No single list of every name exists, and searching one would be slow. Where did a minute-old answer go?

options.text: In your home router's list of where to send packets
options.nudge: Routers work with addresses, not names. Think about what your own device did a minute ago.

cards.explanation: Your device keeps recent answers in a short-term memory called a **cache**. If you looked up example.com a minute ago, the address is probably still there, so no question needs to leave your device at all. That's why many lookups take almost no time.
cards.hint: You already asked this exact question a minute ago. Where might that answer still be?

cards.title: The resolver's trip
cards.body:
First, your device checks its **cache**. If the answer isn't there, it asks a **resolver**: a [[server]] that hunts for answers for you. The resolver asks from general to specific:

1. A **root server** points to the `.com` servers.
2. A **[[TLD]] server** points to example.com's own server.
3. That **authoritative server** holds the real answer.

cards.prompt: Nobody has looked up example.com recently. Put the steps of the lookup in order.

items.label: Your device checks its own cache
The resolver asks a root server who handles .com
The resolver asks a .com server who's in charge of example.com
The resolver asks example.com's authoritative server for the address
The answer comes back, and copies are kept in the caches

cards.explanation: Your device always checks its **cache** first. Then the resolver goes from general to specific: **root**, then **TLD**, then the **authoritative** server, which is the only one that actually holds example.com's address. Finally, copies are saved so the next lookup is instant.
cards.hint: Start with the quickest check that never leaves your device. Then the resolver goes from the most general server to the most specific.
cards.nudge: Your device always looks in its own memory before asking anyone. After that, think country, then town, then street.

cards.prompt: Match each [[DNS]] server to its job.

pairs.right: Does the asking for you and caches answers
Knows where to find each TLD's servers
Knows who's in charge of each domain

cards.explanation: The **resolver** works for you. **Root** servers point to the TLD servers, **TLD** servers point to each domain's authoritative server, and the **authoritative** server holds the real answer. Your device and the resolver only keep *copies* in their caches, and those copies came from the authoritative server in the first place.
cards.hint: Only one server holds the real records. The others either ask for you or point the way to the next server.
cards.nudge: Picture the trip: one server works for you, one points to TLDs, one points to domains, and one holds the actual answer.

cards.prompt:
A cached answer can't be kept forever: the website might move to a new address. So every [[DNS]] answer comes with a **TTL** (time to live): how many **seconds** it may stay in a [[cache]] before it must be looked up again.

An answer has a TTL of **3,600**. How many **minutes** can it be cached for?
cards.explanation: DNS TTLs are in seconds, and there are 60 seconds in a minute, so 3,600 ÷ 60 = **60 minutes**: one hour. After that, the answer is thrown away and looked up fresh. If you typed 3,600, that's the number of seconds.
cards.hint: The TTL is in seconds. How many seconds are in a minute? Divide by that.
cards.nudge: The TTL is in seconds, but the question asks for minutes. Make sure you converted, rather than typing the seconds.

cards.prompt: `dig` is another tool for [[DNS]] lookups. Run `dig example.com`, then find the **TTL**: it's the number just after the name in the answer.
cards.intro: Simulated Linux terminal, with dig's output shortened to just the answer. Type help to see the commands you can use here.

commands.description: Look up example.com and show the answer

success.question: What is the TTL of this answer, in seconds?

cards.explanation: The answer line reads `example.com. 1800 IN A 198.51.100.10`. That's the name, the **TTL** (1,800 seconds, which is 30 minutes), `IN A` (a kind of answer that holds an internet address), and the [[IP address]] itself. The dot after `example.com.` is just how dig writes a full name.
cards.hint: Find the line under `;; ANSWER SECTION:` and look at the number right after the name.
cards.nudge: Don't type the address. The TTL comes straight after `example.com.`, before `IN`.

cards.prompt: At **11:50** you look up a website, and the answer has a TTL of **3,600**. At **12:00** the website moves to a new [[IP address]]. By what time can you be sure your device will use the new address?

options.nudge: Nothing tells your cache that the site moved. It keeps the old answer until its TTL runs out.
The TTL started when you looked the name up, not when the website moved. Count from your lookup.

options.text: Never: the old address is cached forever
options.nudge: Cached answers can't be kept forever. The TTL says exactly how long they may be kept.

cards.explanation:
Your device may keep the old answer for 3,600 seconds (one hour) from when it got it: **11:50 + 1 hour = 12:50**. After that it must look the name up again and gets the new address. It won't happen at 12:00, because nothing tells your cache the site moved. It's also not 13:00, because the hour started when you looked it up, not when the site moved.

TTL is the rule, but in practice some apps and [[resolvers|resolver]] cache a little differently (for example, a [[browser]] may keep its own copy for a short time), so real changes can take slightly longer to reach everyone. That's why website owners often lower the TTL before a move.
cards.hint: The TTL clock starts when your device got the answer. Work out how long 3,600 seconds is, then add it to that time.

cards.title: Recap
cards.body:
- Your device checks its **cache**, then asks a **resolver**.
- The resolver asks root, TLD, then the **authoritative** server.
- Answers stay cached for their **TTL**, counted in seconds.
